extracted.intended_audience: writers of American literary prose and poetry (authors considering use of dialect and style choices)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on stylistic choices for American literary writers: use of dialect, simplicity, satire, and avoiding pedantic or journalistic puffery. Covers criteria for authentic voice, moral purpose, and lively language in prose and verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnest and definite purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requisite of good writing is to have an earnest and definite purpose, whether æsthetic or moral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowell asserts that an author should write with a clear, serious purpose rather than mere jesting. Purpose gives writing weight and direction and helps satire or humor serve a higher end rather than being mere entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination or common-sense for lasting appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Even good writing, to please long, must have more than an average amount either of imagination or common-sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To endure, writing needs either extraordinary imaginative power (rare) or above-average common-sense (attainable by many). Aim to supply one of these qualities to give work staying power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialect from living sources (authentic speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only from its roots in the living generations of men that a language can be reinforced with fresh vigor for its needs; our popular idiom is racy with life and vigor, ... not a mere graft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on genuine popular speech as a source of freshness and originality. The Yankee dialect is praised as a living source that can energize literature; using dialect can give authenticity and vigor when handled with understanding of its roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance dialect with higher register where needed
rubrics_metrics.description: When I needed on occasion to rise above the level of mere patois, I conceived the Rev. Mr. Wilbur ... as Mr. Biglow should serve for its homely common-sense vivified and heated by conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid limiting yourself to patois when the subject or moral scope requires more nuance. Use complementary voices/characters (e.g., a parson or another persona) to provide contrasts and to express views the dialect speaker may not convey well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vulgarizing conviction when using comic or homely forms
rubrics_metrics.description: On the one hand, I was in danger of being carried beyond the limit of my own opinions, or at least of that temper with which every man should speak his mind in print, and on the other I feared the risk of seeming to vulgarize a deep and sacred conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor and dialect should not be used to make serious convictions seem trivial. Maintain moral seriousness beneath the comic or homely surface so that satire instructs rather than merely amuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, directness, and precision of English
rubrics_metrics.description: The great vice of American writing and speaking was a studied want of simplicity, that we were in danger of coming to look on our mother-tongue as a dead language, to be sought in the grammar and dictionary rather than in the heart. President Lincoln ... was master ... of a truly masculine English, classic, because it was of no special period, and level at once to the highest and lowest of his countrymen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for plain, direct, and precise language (a 'masculine' classic English in Lowell's terms) that can reach broad audiences. Simplicity is a virtue that lends force and clarity; cultivate it through reading exemplars like Lincoln, Shakespeare, Milton, and the Bible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pedantic, 'starched' bookish diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where language is too strictly limited by convention, the ground for expression to grow in is limited also; and we get a potted literature, Chinese dwarfs instead of healthy trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making prose that sounds like a bookish exercise rather than living speech. Beware the 'Universal Schoolmaster' who enforces models that strip language of warmth; prefer lively idiom over pedantic correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid newspaper puffery and inflated euphemisms (journalese)
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper reporter has been doing even more harm by stretching and swelling [language] to suit his occasions. [Examples given in paired columns: Old Style -> New Style, e.g., 'Was hanged.' -> 'Was launched into eternity.'; 'House burned.' -> 'Edifice consumed.' etc.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of the grandiose, inflated phrasings common in journalism (e.g., 'the progress of the devouring element was arrested' instead of 'the fire was got under'). Lowell gives many paired examples to illustrate how simple statements become pompous; prefer plain truthful phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wire-drawn figurative language and overdone metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: The school of Pope in verse ended by wire-drawing its phrase to such thinness that it could bear no weight of meaning whatever. ... I will not waste time in criticising the bad English or the mixture of metaphor in these sentences ... 'The shadowy phantom of the Republic continued to flit before the eyes of the Cæsar.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't force or overwork figurative language until it becomes thin or absurd. Let metaphors be fresh and apt; avoid convoluted horticultural or mixed metaphors that obscure meaning rather than illuminate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize satire to increase lasting value
rubrics_metrics.description: I endeavored, by generalising my satire, to give it what value I could beyond the passing moment and the immediate application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make satire speak to larger principles rather than only the immediate target. Generalization helps satire remain relevant beyond topical moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite humor with moral conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: I conceive that true humor is never divorced from moral conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comic writing or humorous persona should be informed by an underlying ethical stance; humor grounded in conscience carries greater weight and avoids mere frivolity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration can be legitimate intensity and raw material for art
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of exaggeration has often been remarked on as typical of American character ... a great deal of what is set down as mere extravagance is more fitly to be called intensity and picturesqueness, symptoms of the imaginative faculty in full health and strength, though producing, as yet, only the raw and formless material in which poetry is to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reflexively condemn strong or 'exaggerated' expression: it may be a necessary stage of imaginative growth and supply raw material for refined poetry and art. Harness intensity judiciously rather than suppressing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulgarity resides in thought, not in word; don't fear popular expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Properly speaking, vulgarity is in the thought, and not in the word or the way of pronouncing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using rustic or popular phrases is not inherently vulgar; evaluate moral quality of ideas rather than surface diction. Bold or colloquial phrasing can be legitimate and valuable if the underlying thought is sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language is the soil of thought — nourish writing from communal speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is the soil of thought, and our own especially is a rich leaf-mould ... True vigor and heartiness of phrase do not pass from page to page, but from man to man ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat language as living cultural material. Engage with communal, everyday speech to cultivate lively expression; writing refreshed from social speech will be more vital than that confined to abstract 'correct' models.
